EdgeDesk makes it Duke -37.3 before any sportsbook number is consulted, with Duke winning 99% of simulations.

The roster and position-group comparison below explains where EdgeDesk’s separation comes from on the side it can measure; William & Mary is absent from the FBS player dataset, so the exact size of that gap is not established.
Data confidence on this matchup is 38% — enough to publish, not enough to treat the exact margin as settled.

advantages.note: An advantage is only claimed where BOTH teams carry a national rank in that category — the national rank is the one scale on which a QB room and a run defence are comparable. A category where one side is unrated appears here as a measurement and as uncertainty, never as an edge.

favourite.heading: Why Duke can pull away
bullets: Duke is the better football team by 33.2 points on opponent-adjusted results — but about 74% of that rating is still last season carried forward, and in a portal era last season is a different team (+33.2 pts).
Playing at Duke is worth 4.1 points — the league-wide home-field number, because a per-venue table was tested and could not be told apart from the home team’s own quality (+4.1 pts).

underdog.heading: Why William & Mary can keep it close
bullets: The outcome range is 15.3 points wide at one sigma — p10 +14.3 to p90 +58.3 for Duke, so a projection of +37.3 still produces results a long way either side of it.
It is early enough that both ratings still lean on preseason belief — it widens the outcome range by about 4%.
60% of the model’s own input contract was empty for this game — no starter, injury, schedule or per-player talent context reached it, so the number leans on team strength more than it should.
William & Mary is not in the FBS rating set, so EdgeDesk cannot measure what it does well. An unmeasured opponent is an unknown, not a weak one, and the size of the gap is not established.
